Generative Artificial Intelligence Reshapes Academic Publishing and Strains Peer Review Integrity

Academic peer-reviewed publishing is experiencing severe operational strain as generative artificial intelligence sharply lowers the cost of producing scientific manuscripts while leaving reviewer evaluation capacity increasingly constrained. In an editorial published in Business and Information Systems Engineering, researchers Björn Hanneke, Frederik Hering, Jella Pfeiffer, Hajo Reijers, and Oliver Hinz analyze how cognitive automation threatens the three finite resources that sustain scholarly certification: editorial attention, referee availability, and reader attention. Across the scholarly communication landscape, journals are confronted with rapid submission growth, rising noise-to-signal ratios, and expanding screening burdens. At Business and Information Systems Engineering alone, annual submissions expanded from 96 manuscripts in 2010 to 602 in 2025, roughly doubling between 2020 and 2025. Over the identical timeframe, the journal’s overall acceptance rate contracted sharply from 11.3 percent in 2020 to 3.8 percent in 2025. Because automated text generation allows authors to assemble polished, submission-ready papers with unprecedented speed, journal backlogs are no longer governed by author writing time, shifting the primary systemic bottleneck entirely to unpaid volunteer peer reviewers.

The authors conceptualize this structural transformation by examining cognitive automation, defined as the execution of tasks traditionally classified as cognitive work, such as searching literature, formulating hypotheses, generating code, running statistical models, writing text, and assembling reviewer responses. To clarify the expanding technological frontier, the editorial establishes a taxonomy of three distinct stages of artificial intelligence deployment across research workflows. Stage one encompasses ad hoc prompting of general-purpose foundation models to produce outlines, draft sections, generate tables, and write initial computer code. Stage two involves structured collaboration with task-specific systems executing defined functions within partially standardized processes, including citation validation, claim-to-evidence mapping, automated robustness testing, and simulated peer review. Stage three represents a qualitative shift toward fully engineered, autonomous agentic pipelines that conduct end-to-end knowledge generation. In this advanced stage, multi-agent architectures autonomously retrieve background literature, formulate experimental hypotheses, execute analyses, stress-test computational outputs, and write narrative manuscripts with traceable evidence links, moving human researchers from direct artifact writing to system engineering.

Stage one adoption is already widespread, backed by measurable productivity gains documented in controlled experiments across professional settings. In an empirical study involving 453 college-educated professionals, ChatGPT access reduced task completion time by 40 percent while simultaneously raising output quality evaluations by 18 percent. Similarly, a field deployment tracking 5,172 customer-support representatives measured a 15 percent mean efficiency gain, and an investigation of management consultants using GPT-4 documented a 12.2 percent increase in completed tasks alongside a 40 percent quality boost within the technology frontier. Within academic settings, artificial intelligence tools applied to reanalyzing published economics literature reproduced primary econometric results substantially faster than manual methods while surfacing methodological inconsistencies overlooked by original human peer reviewers. These efficiencies lower drafting friction and revision expenses for academic authors, but they decouple writing fluency from underlying scholarly rigor. Authors can readily generate grammatically pristine text that masks conceptual ambiguity, defective methodologies, or unverified claims, ultimately eroding surface prose quality as a reliable screening signal for journal editors.

The risks inherent to stage one stem directly from the underlying architecture of contemporary foundation models, which perform probabilistic pattern matching rather than epistemic reasoning or conceptual comprehension. These systems represent information stylistically rather than faithfully, lacking epistemic agency despite generating polished prose. Consequently, artificial intelligence outputs routinely propagate subtle errors, flawed code snippets, and hallucinated citations that can compound across citations and degrade cumulative scientific literature. For editorial offices, polished low-quality submissions create heavy administrative overhead, demanding extended screening times while driving up desk rejection frequencies. Editorial boards are responding by tightening accountability frameworks and enforcing strict rejection rules for papers containing hallucinated bibliographic references. Certain institutions, including dissertation committees at German universities and preprint platforms such as arXiv, have already introduced automatic rejection policies or formal submission bans for authors submitting manuscripts containing fabricated citations, establishing precedents for peer-reviewed journal governance.

Stage two broadens these capabilities by integrating retrieval-augmented generation and tool-augmented artificial intelligence into specialized research pipelines. Retrieval mechanisms query external databases at runtime to verify assertions against primary records, while tool-calling integrations invoke statistical packages, execution sandboxes, and application programming interfaces. Applied researchers already deploy these tools for econometric causal inference and financial modeling. However, technical evaluations demonstrate that retrieval-augmented generation remains vulnerable to retrieval failures, while sequential tool chaining causes minor operational errors to multiply. A rigorous benchmark evaluating 19 contemporary large language models established that frontier architectures silently corrupt roughly 25 percent of document content across extended delegated workflows. This corruption rate worsens as document size and interaction length increase, and it fails to improve when agentic tool functionality is enabled. Furthermore, commercial access costs for specialized tools threaten to widen disparities between well-funded and resource-constrained institutions, while standardized prompts risk homogenizing scholarly methodologies.

Stage three introduces autonomous knowledge production through interacting multi-agent environments where modular agents divide labor into specialized functions, including literature searching, code execution, and adversarial criticism. Prototype systems such as the Automated Peer Evaluator, the End-to-End Researcher, Sakana AI Scientist version two, zeropaper, paper orchestrator, and ARIS demonstrate the technical feasibility of end-to-end automated scientific pipelines. However, multi-agent complexity creates severe hazards, including error cascades across sequential subtasks, uninterpretable emergent behaviors, and diffused researcher accountability. Empirical investigations reveal that self-generated reasoning traces generated by language models frequently diverge from their internal computational operations, producing unfaithful explanations. In more extreme self-modifying architectures, designated as stage three star, pipelines dynamically alter their own configurations via reinforcement learning or automated component selection. Such dynamic modifications severely undermine scientific reproducibility, as the algorithmic system operating at submission may no longer correspond to the pipeline configuration that originally produced the reported empirical findings.
